meta.scope_note: Middle school (6-8) and a grounded slice of high school Algebra/Functions -- only the strands and specific codes a real read of Bootstrap:Algebra's own 28-lesson sequence (bootstrapworld.org, Fall 2026 course page) actually supports, not every code its domain could theoretically cover. Skipped entirely, for lack of any matching lesson: A-SSE other than A-SSE.1 (quadratics/exponential series), A-REI.1/2/4 (quadratics), F-IF.3, F-IF.5-6, F-IF.8-9 (sequences, complex curve analysis, quadratic/exponential forms), F-BF.2-4 (sequences, transformations, inverses), F-LE.3-4 (exponential-specific), Grades 6-8 Statistics & Probability codes in this catalog (6.SP, 7.SP.A.1, 8.SP) are NOT claimed by Bootstrap:Algebra, whose lessons never analyze real-world data; they exist for the Hour of Data lesson (hour-of-data.json), added 2026-11-07 together with 6.RP.A.3, 7.RP.A.3 and S-ID.6, the three codes Bootstrap's own Hour of Data tags name that the catalog lacked. Not a general-purpose math catalog -- no other Ratios & Proportions, no Geometry outside the two codes grounded here, no untouched high school content. Add strands as a real need shows up, the same way this project's ccss-ela.json stayed scoped to what was actually cited. Added 2026-11-07 from the full Bootstrap:Algebra student workbook (attic/bootstrap_algebra_workbook.pdf): 6.EE.2, 6.EE.9, 8.F.4, 8.F.5, F-IF.4 and A-SSE.1.
meta.codes_note: Codes are CCSS's own (e.g. 6.NS.5, 8.F.2), not a project-specific scheme. Lettered sub-parts (e.g. 6.NS.6.a-c, 7.EE.4.a-b) are folded into one paraphrase per numbered standard, matching this project's existing topic-level citation granularity (see apcsp.json's topic/LO split, or ccss-ela.json's own codes_note).

items.paraphrase: Use positive and negative numbers to represent quantities with opposite directions or values (temperature, elevation, debits/credits), explaining what 0 means in context.
Understand rational numbers as points on a number line, extend number lines and coordinate axes to negative numbers, and locate points in all four quadrants of the coordinate plane.
Understand ordering and absolute value of rational numbers, including that absolute value is a number's distance from 0.
Solve real-world problems by graphing points in all four quadrants of the coordinate plane, using coordinates and absolute value to find distances between points sharing a coordinate.
Recognize a statistical question as one that anticipates variability in the data.
Understand that a data set has a distribution describable by center, spread, and overall shape.
Recognize that a measure of center summarizes a data set with a single number, and a measure of variation describes its spread with a single number.

Summarize numerical data sets in context: report the number of observations, describe the attribute measured, give quantitative measures of center and variability, and relate the choice of measures to the shape of the distribution.
Use properties of operations to add, subtract, factor, and expand linear expressions with rational coefficients.
Recognize that rewriting an expression in a different form can clarify a problem and how its quantities relate.
Solve multi-step real-life problems with rational numbers in any form, using properties of operations and checking the reasonableness of answers.
Use variables to represent quantities, write equations and inequalities to solve real-world problems, and graph and interpret inequality solution sets.
Understand that statistics can be used to gain information about a population by examining a representative sample, typically through random sampling.
Understand a function as a rule that assigns exactly one output to each input; a function's graph is the set of ordered pairs of input and output.
Compare properties of two functions represented in different ways (algebraically, graphically, in a table, or by verbal description).
Interpret the equation y = mx + b as defining a linear function, and give examples of functions that are not linear.
Explain a proof of the Pythagorean Theorem and its converse.
Apply the Pythagorean Theorem to determine unknown side lengths in right triangles, in real-world and mathematical problems in two and three dimensions.
Apply the Pythagorean Theorem to find the distance between two points in a coordinate system.
Construct and interpret scatter plots for bivariate measurement data to investigate patterns such as clustering, outliers, and association.
Know that straight lines are widely used to model relationships between two quantitative variables; informally fit a line to data that suggests a linear association.
Use the equation of a fitted linear model to solve problems in the context of bivariate measurement data, interpreting the slope and intercept.
Represent three-dimensional figures using nets of rectangles and triangles, and use nets to find surface area.
Describe the effect of dilations, translations, rotations, and reflections on two-dimensional figures using coordinates.
A function assigns each input in its domain exactly one output in its range; f(x) denotes the output for input x.
Use function notation, evaluate functions at inputs in their domains, and interpret statements that use function notation in context.
Graph functions expressed symbolically, including piecewise-defined functions (step and absolute value functions among them), showing key features.
Write a function that describes a relationship between two quantities, including composing functions (using one function's output as another's input).
Write equations and inequalities in one variable, including linear ones, to solve problems.
Write equations in two or more variables to represent relationships between quantities, and graph them on labeled axes.
Use equations, inequalities, or systems of them to represent constraints in a context, and judge whether a solution is workable given those constraints.

groups.name: High School: Reasoning with Equations & Inequalities

items.paraphrase: Solve linear equations and inequalities in one variable, including those with coefficients given as letters.
Understand that the graph of an equation in two variables is the set of all its solutions plotted in the coordinate plane.
Graph the solution to a linear inequality in two variables as a half-plane, and graph the solution to a system of linear inequalities as the intersection of the corresponding half-planes.
Distinguish situations modeled by linear functions (equal differences over equal intervals) from those modeled by exponential functions (equal factors over equal intervals).
Construct linear and exponential functions from a graph, a description of a relationship, or two input-output pairs.
Interpret the parameters of a linear or exponential function (e.g. slope, intercept) in terms of the context it models.

Use ratio and rate reasoning to solve real-world problems, including finding a percent of a quantity as a rate per 100 and solving unit-rate and measurement problems with tables, tape diagrams, or double number lines.
Use proportional relationships to solve multi-step ratio and percent problems, such as scaling a known rate up to predict an unknown amount, percent increase and decrease, and percent error.

groups.name: High School: Interpreting Categorical & Quantitative Data

items.paraphrase: Represent two-variable data on a scatter plot, look for the overall pattern and for points that break it, and describe how well a function fits the data.
Write, read and evaluate expressions in which letters stand for numbers, naming the parts of an expression and evaluating it by following the order of operations.

Use variables to represent two quantities that change in relationship to one another, writing an equation for the dependent variable in terms of the independent one and relating it to a table and a graph.
Build a function that models a linear relationship, find its rate of change and starting value from a table, graph or description, and say what they mean in the situation.
Describe in words how two quantities are related by reading a graph (where it rises, falls, or levels off), and sketch a graph that matches a described story.

groups.name: High School: Seeing Structure in Expressions

items.paraphrase: Interpret an expression by naming its parts (terms, factors, coefficients) and, for a longer one, by viewing a piece of it as a single quantity.
For a function that models a relationship, interpret key features of its graph or table (intercepts, where it increases or decreases) in terms of the quantities involved.
